lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: What is the Temporal Dead Zone in JavaScript?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: It is a short period where a variable already exists, but you are not allowed to use it yet. Let us see why.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Before JavaScript runs your code, it reads through the scope, and creates a box in memory for every variable. This step is called hoisting.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Only after that, it runs your lines, one at a time.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: A {var} box is created early, and filled with {undefined}.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: So reading it too soon does not fail. You just get {undefined}.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Then the line runs, and the box gets its real value.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: A {let} box is also created early. But it is locked.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: It stays locked, until the line that declares it runs.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Read it while it is locked, and JavaScript throws a ReferenceError.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The message says: cannot access b before initialization.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The time while the box is locked, is the Temporal Dead Zone.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Does [typeof|type of|c] protect me?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Not inside the dead zone. [typeof|type of|c] on a locked variable throws too.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: It only gives {undefined} for names that were never declared at all.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: So is it about where the code is written?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: No. It is about when the program runs.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: This function reads x, and it works, because it runs after the declaration.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Any interview trap?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Yes. Shadowing. An outer x exists, and the block declares its own x, using {let}.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The whole block is now in the dead zone for that name, so reading x above the declaration throws.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The same rule applies to {const}, and to {class} declarations.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The dead zone turns silent bugs into loud errors. That is why {let} and {const} are safer than {var}.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Got it. Same variable, but with a guard.
